$comment: Committed reference points for tests/e2e/mobile/chat-render-perf.spec.ts. The spec writes
each run to the gitignored test-results/; this file is what to diff against.
Absolute timings are machine-bound (Apple Silicon laptop, Turbopack dev server) — read the
RATIOS. `jsHeapUsedBytes` is a single GC-dependent sample and swings 2x between identical
runs; treat it as an order of magnitude, not a measurement. The two numbers that are stable
enough to gate a judgement on are `scrollHeightDriftPx` (structural, not timing-dependent)
Caveat on imageBytes: the seeder encodes full-frame noise, the worst case for a given
resolution — a real UI screenshot has flat regions and compresses better. The perf tier's
72MB across 40 frames is closer to what ~150 real 1568px screenshots weigh. The
SWEEP CHANGE: `preChange` was captured with a fraction-of-range sweep; every entry here
uses the screen-at-a-time sweep that replaced it. Improving the row-height estimator
changes the virtual total, so a fraction-based sweep silently covers more content per step
and reports the extra work as a regression. Only same-sweep rows compare.

reading: scrollHeightDriftPx 8399 → 2866 (-66%): the content-derived row estimate is close enough that the virtualizer stops rewriting its own total as rows scroll in. This is the metric the estimator moves, and it is not timing-dependent.
Everything else is inside single-sample noise. This tier is image-dominated — 72MB of base64 across 40 frames — and none of the render-layer work touches that. Only the storage change can.

preRenderHardening_OLD_SWEEP.sweep: fraction-of-range — NOT comparable to the row below

reading: Long-task total 27.1s → 13.5s and React commit time 18.2s → 9.7s. The sweep changed between these two runs, so read the direction, not the exact ratio; the code-fence and table budgets are separately pinned by unit tests.
The single worst long task barely moved (9179 → 8851ms). That one is open-time work dominated by deserializing and decoding 717MB of inlined base64 — untouched by anything in the render layer.

jsHeapUsedBytes went UP (1.86 → 2.24GB). Not a regression to chase: it is one GC-dependent sample, and the surrounding numbers all improved. A real iOS WKWebView (~1-1.5GB per tab) is OOM-killed at either figure, which is the actual finding.
Verdict: render-layer hardening removes the multi-second scroll stalls but cannot make this tier viable. The payload has to shrink.
